NEW YORK (CNN) -- Reigning hot dog-guzzling champ Joey Chestnut and nemesis Takeru Kobayashi of Japan attempted to psych each other out Thursday at the weigh-in for the 94th annual Nathan's Famous Fourth of July International Hot Dog-Eating Contest. It was Chestnut's second slim victory over Kobayashi in as many years. Kobayashi vowed he will avenge those two defeats on Saturday. He also said he no longer suffers from the "jawthritis" that some cited as the culprit for his 2007 defeat, which snapped his six-year winning streak at Coney Island. Chestnut, for his part, said he had no intention of ceding the coveted mustard yellow belt -- competitive eating's answer to golf's green jacket. He is setting his sights this year on 68 hot dogs in 10 minutes. Saturday's competition will be partially about redemption for Chestnut, too. In May, he suffered a stinging defeat to Kobayashi in a loss he said "really set a fire underneath me" and "made me hungry for this contest." Chestnut revealed the extreme dietary regimen he is following in the days leading up to the contest. He said he is sticking to water to make sure he is "empty" when the mountain of hot dogs is placed in front of him. In addition to Chestnut, Kobayashi admitted to keeping a watchful eye on 32-year-old Tim "Eater X" Janus, whose signature painted face was described by Major League Eating impresario Richard Shea as an attempt to mask his "inner torment." In a recent trial round, Janus downed a personal-best 55 hot dogs -- a weiner's throw from the 59 that Chestnut and Kobayashi wolfed down last year. As a lead-in to the main event, Major League Eating on Friday will hold a first-of-its-kind "cross-species" eating contest between three competitive eaters and three Asian elephants. MLE's Shea described it as the realization of one of his two lifelong dreams, the other being a scenario in which a dozen competitive eaters eat the entire contents of a convenience store. Twenty finalists will compete in the championship on Saturday. They were culled from 18 preliminary contests and comprise a Who's Who of the world of competitive eating. For people who stuff their faces with record-breaking quantities of food, many of the contestants at the weigh-in boasted surprisingly svelte physiques. Juliet Lee, a 44-year-old Maryland salon owner fresh off the feat of downing 13.23 pounds of cranberry sauce in 8 minutes, clocked in at a mere 105 pounds. Kobayashi, at 123 pounds, lifted his T-shirt to reveal the sort of chiseled abdomen one would expect at a bodybuilding competition. Others contestants were not quite as disconcertingly trim. Fearsome world matzo ball-eating champion Eric "Badlands" Booker tips the scales at 400 pounds.

Chestnut described the extreme dietary regimen he is following in the days leading up to the event. He said he is consuming only water to ensure he is “empty” when the mountain of hot dogs is placed before him.

In addition to Kobayashi, Chestnut admitted he is keeping a watchful eye on 32-year-old Tim “Eater X” Janus, whose signature painted face was described by Major League Eating impresario Richard Shea as an attempt to mask his “inner torment.”

NEW YORK (CNN) — Joey Chestnut, the current hot dog-eating champion, and his Japanese rival, Takeru Kobayashi, tried to get inside each other’s heads Thursday during the weigh-in for the 94th annual Nathan’s Famous Fourth of July International Hot Dog-Eating Contest.

The two competitive eating stars participated in an official “staredown,” locking eyes for a long, intimidating glare.

In last year’s competition, Chestnut, then 25 and a civil engineering student at San Jose State University, narrowly defeated 31-year-old Kobayashi in a tiebreaker after both men had first eaten 59 hot dogs. That marked Chestnut’s second close win over Kobayashi in two consecutive years.

Kobayashi said he intends to get revenge for those back-to-back losses on Saturday. He also said he is no longer dealing with the “jawthritis” that some blamed for his 2007 loss, the defeat that ended his six-year winning streak at Coney Island.

Chestnut, meanwhile, made it clear that he does not plan to give up the prized mustard-yellow belt, the competitive eating equivalent of golf’s green jacket. This year, he is aiming to eat 68 hot dogs in 10 minutes.

Saturday’s contest also carries a chance at redemption for Chestnut. In May, Kobayashi handed him a painful loss, which Chestnut said “really set a fire underneath me” and “made me hungry for this contest.”

Chestnut also described the intense diet he is using in the final days before the event. He said he is consuming only water so that he will be “empty” when the pile of hot dogs is put in front of him.

Kobayashi, along with Chestnut, acknowledged that he is also paying close attention to 32-year-old Tim “Eater X” Janus. Janus is known for his painted face, which Major League Eating showman Richard Shea described as an effort to conceal his “inner torment.”

In a recent qualifying round, Janus ate a personal record of 55 hot dogs, putting him within reach of the 59 hot dogs Chestnut and Kobayashi consumed the previous year.

Before the main competition, Major League Eating plans to stage an unusual first on Friday: a “cross-species” eating contest featuring three competitive eaters against three Asian elephants. Shea of MLE called the event the fulfillment of one of his two lifelong dreams. His other dream, he said, is to see 12 competitive eaters consume everything inside a convenience store.

On Saturday, 20 finalists will take part in the championship. They were selected from 18 qualifying events and represent many of the biggest names in competitive eating.

Despite their ability to consume record-setting amounts of food, many competitors at the weigh-in had unexpectedly lean bodies. Juliet Lee, a 44-year-old salon owner from Maryland who had recently eaten 13.23 pounds of cranberry sauce in eight minutes, weighed only 105 pounds.

Kobayashi, weighing 123 pounds, pulled up his T-shirt to show a sharply defined midsection that looked more suited to a bodybuilding event.

Other competitors were not quite so surprisingly slender. Eric “Badlands” Booker, the formidable world matzo ball-eating champion, weighed in at 400 pounds.

Nathan’s Famous Hot Dog Eating Contest, held annually on July 4 in Coney Island, is sanctioned by Major League Eating and remains the marquee event in competitive eating. Contestants typically dunk buns in water to make them easier to swallow, use rhythmic eating patterns, and train for months to expand capacity and maintain speed. They also cultivate the thousand-yard stare of people who have done serious math involving sodium.

The mental game is no small matter. In a contest where elite eaters can consume dozens of hot dogs and buns in 10 minutes, hesitation is costly. A fraction of a second spent wondering whether the person next to you has discovered “a revolutionary mustard-adjacent mindset” is a fraction of a second not spent eating.

“Everyone’s trying to get in everyone else’s head,” one observer said. “Which is difficult, because most of the available space is already occupied by hot dog logistics.”

Common intimidation tactics include arriving unusually relaxed, overpraising an opponent’s conditioning, or saying things like, “I’m just here to have fun,” which in competitive eating circles is widely understood to mean, “I have trained my esophagus like a carnival strongman.”

Some veterans prefer silence, letting their records do the talking. Others use exaggerated calm, smiling through interviews while refusing to reveal whether they have trained with standard franks, longer franks, softer buns, firmer buns, or the feared “contest simulation,” a phrase that makes casual diners push away from the table.

Still, the atmosphere remains oddly festive. Fans line the boardwalk, cameras crowd the stage, and the competitors — despite the gamesmanship — often speak of one another with genuine respect. Competitive eating may look like chaos with condiments, but at its highest level it requires preparation, pain tolerance, technique, and the ability to remain composed while a nearby adult is dunking bread into water with the focus of a bomb technician.

By contest time, the bravado will be gone, replaced by the wet slap of buns, the churn of the crowd, and the grim arithmetic of hot dog totals. Until then, Coney Island belongs to the feints, flexes, and carefully planted rumors.

Asked whether the mind games work, one competitor reportedly shrugged.
